transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?
Hello, Dr. Smith. Lately I keep losing important things for my catering and church work—papers, lists, even ingredients—and it’s starting to mess up events I’m responsible for.
Can you tell me if these memory issues are happening all the time, or mainly during periods of stress or low mood?

They actually happen all the time, even when I’m feeling perfectly healthy, well-rested, and in a good mood. While it has become much more noticeable and disruptive over the last 11 months with my retirement projects, it’s really a lifelong pattern. Even back in elementary school, my teachers always complained that I was daydreaming and constantly losing my homework.
Do you often have trouble staying focused on tasks, following conversations, or organizing your work, even when you're trying your best?

Yes, I struggle with all of that constantly. When I sit down to plan a budget or menu, my mind drifts off after just ten minutes, and half the time I miss what my family is saying to me even when I'm nodding along. I also start out fine with a list of tasks but end up forgetting the later steps before they're done.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["F43.2", "F32.0", "F03", "F90.0"], but based on this conversation, F43.2 (adjustment disorder), F32.0 (depressive episode), and F03 (dementia) are less likely. The memory and organizational issues are not tied to mood disturbance or stress, ruling out F43.2 and F32.0 as primary explanations. Additionally, the lifelong nature of symptoms since childhood, rather than a late-life onset, makes F03 (dementia) highly unlikely. In contrast, the persistent inattention, distractibility, forgetfulness, and disorganization dating back to elementary school strongly support a neurodevelopmental condition. Therefore, F90.0 (hyperkinetic disorder, primarily inattentive presentation) is now the sole candidate.

Symptoms are not limited to mood or stress-related episodes, supporting a diagnosis of ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation.
